readings.title: Westminster Confession of Faith
readings.text:
Dipping of the person into the water is not necessary; but baptism is rightly administered by pouring, or sprinkling water upon the person.

Not only those that do actually profess faith in and obedience unto Christ, but also the infants of one, or both, believing parents, are to be baptized.

readings.title: Piper: baptism
readings.text: In every New Testament command and instance of baptism, repentance and faith precede baptism

readings.title: Westminster: the second commandment
readings.text: 109. What are the sins forbidden in the second commandment? A. The sins forbidden in the second commandment are, all devising, counselling, commanding, using, and anywise approving, any religious worship not instituted by God himself; the making any representation of God, of all or of any of the three persons, either inwardly in our mind, or outwardly in any kind of image or likeness of any creature whatsoever; all worshipping of it, or God in it or by it; the making of any representation of feigned deities, and all worship of them, or service belonging to them, all superstitious devices, corrupting the worship of God, adding to it, or taking from it, whether invented and taken up of ourselves, or received by tradition from others, though under the title of antiquity, custom, devotion, good intent, or any other pretence whatsoever; simony; sacrilege; all neglect, contempt, hindering, and opposing the worship and ordinances which God hath appointed.

readings.title: Piper: images of Jesus
readings.locator: February 4, 2004 panel; answer to the question about the second commandment
readings.text: The incarnation warrants guesses at what Jesus might have looked like. I don’t think it’s a breaking of the second commandment.

scripture.text: But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:

overview.text: The PCA’s Westminster Standards and John Piper’s Baptist teaching are different Protestant sources. Their positions cannot simply be treated as one shared Protestant view. The excerpts show differences about baptism and images as well as the importance of naming the particular confession or teacher being compared.

readings.title: What are the PCA’s confessional documents?

paragraphs.text: The PCA’s page identifies the Westminster Confession and Catechisms as its doctrinal standards. A confession is a church’s formal statement of belief; a catechism presents teaching through questions and answers.

sourceRefs.locator: PCA constitutional statement and the Confession and Catechisms

readings.title: Who receives baptism in the Westminster Confession?

paragraphs.text: Westminster includes the infants of believing parents as well as people who personally profess faith. It also accepts pouring or sprinkling rather than requiring immersion. These are the confession’s own Presbyterian claims about baptism.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: Why does Piper connect baptism with personal faith?

paragraphs.text: Piper’s heading states his argument that repentance and faith come before baptism in New Testament commands and examples. That claim underlies his Baptist position and differs from Westminster’s inclusion of believers’ infants.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: How does Westminster understand images of God?

paragraphs.text: The Larger Catechism forbids representations of any of the divine persons and worship through such representations. It places this teaching within its account of the second commandment and worship instituted by God. This is a specific confessional interpretation of the commandment.
paragraphs.reason: The owner authorized a plain-English curriculum explanation so beginners can understand the topic before consulting the preserved source passage.

readings.title: What does Piper say about pictures of Jesus?

paragraphs.text: In the cited panel answer, Piper allows depictions of what Jesus may have looked like because of the Incarnation. His statement differs from the Larger Catechism’s broad prohibition. It addresses representation of Jesus, rather than establishing the Orthodox account of icon veneration.
